description:
Six dual students from DHBW Stuttgart, working at Bosch, TRUMPF and IBM, with a focus on data science, one of us also on the Formula Student team. We’re here because we love building stuff, and this weekend that means hacking with NASA data.
We are "Overfitted & Overwhelmed"!
summary:
AGRIscora is an explorer for crop rotations, not a black box that tells a farmer what to plant. The farmer picks their field on a map, chooses the crops they can grow and sets what matters to them: saving water, low weather risk, soil health, less fertilizer. AGRIscora then scores ~200 three-year rotations, with and without a winter cover crop, on 35 years of NASA weather for that exact spot, and shows the current rotation side by side with the best matches, month by month. The farmer can also build their own rotation (drag crops onto years, add a cover crop) and see it scored live on the same scale. For every option the tool explains why it fits, what the evidence is and what a local expert should check.

Example field: Kearny County, Kansas. Satellite crop maps show corn on this field every summer since 2008. Compared with continuous corn, the best match (sorghum – sorghum – sunflower with a triticale cover crop) needs about 33 % less irrigation water (12.6 vs. 18.9 inches per year), the share of bare-soil days drops from 47 % to 9 %, and nitrogen fertilizer drops from 266 to 166 lb per acre and year. These are model estimates for farmers and local experts to review, not prescriptions.

The prototype starts with one field to keep every number traceable. The method is location-independent: NASA POWER and the FAO crop data cover the whole globe, so a new region needs its crop list, crop calendar and soil map. AGRIscora shows what 35 years of data say. The farmer decides.
details:
AGRIscora is a decision-support tool that helps farmers adapt their crop rotations to a changing climate. A farmer opens the web dashboard, finds their field on the map and enters the rotation they grow today. AGRIscora then compares it with the best alternative multi-year rotations on four criteria: irrigation water need, climate risk from heat and cold stress, nitrogen fertilizer need, and soil health, measured as the days the soil lies bare and can erode.

It starts with NASA POWER daily weather for 1991–2025 (precipitation, minimum, maximum and mean temperature, solar radiation and humidity). From these we compute reference evapotranspiration with the FAO-56 Penman-Monteith method. Our Crop Scorer builds every ordered three-crop rotation from corn, sorghum, soybean, sunflower and winter wheat, 125 rotations in total. Wherever a gap between two crops allows it, each rotation also gets a variant with a triticale cover crop, for 225 candidates.

Every candidate is replayed over about 33 historical weather years. Sowing and harvest dates come from USDA NASS crop calendars, including double crops and skipped years. A daily FAO-56 soil-water balance on SSURGO soil data gives the irrigation need. Ecocrop temperature limits give the heat stress, cold stress and winter-kill days. K-State MF2586 equations, adjusted for the previous crop and for the cover crop, give the nitrogen need. Rules from extension guides are applied as well, such as the NDSU recommendation of at most one white mold (Sclerotinia) host per rotation.

A FastAPI explorer service re-ranks all candidates with the weights the farmer sets for the four criteria. For each rotation it returns yields with 10th–90th percentile ranges, monthly water and stress values, and the source of every number. The React dashboard presents this in four tabs:

- Field: USDA Cropland Data Layer crop history and live Sentinel-2 NDVI computed in the browser.

- Plan: a drag-and-drop rotation builder with a cover crop switch.

- Compare: rotations side by side.

- Data: every source and assumption.

As a prototype, we also built a Model Context Protocol server and an LLM chatbot backend. Farmers, or AI assistants, can ask questions in their own words, such as why one rotation beats another or what changes if water matters most. The answers are built only from the tool outputs, and guardrails stop the model from inventing numbers.

What benefits does it have?

AGRIscora puts water, risk, fertilizer and soil protection on the same days and the same 35 years of real weather, so the trade-offs are directly comparable. Instead of a single average it shows how a rotation does across good and bad years. The ranking follows the farmer's own priorities rather than one fixed idea of what is optimal. Every number can be traced to its source and the assumptions are listed openly in the interface. The tool runs in the browser on public data, so farmers don't need to install or pay for anything.

What is the intended impact?

Our pilot field is in Kearny County, Kansas. It sits over the depleting Ogallala aquifer, where irrigation water is the limiting resource and summer heat stress is rising. We want farmers to see in concrete numbers how a different rotation or a cover crop changes their water use, fertilizer cost, climate risk and soil protection, so that adaptation becomes a decision based on evidence rather than a gamble. Saving groundwater, cutting nitrogen losses and keeping soil covered also helps the whole region. AGRIscora is meant to open a conversation, not replace one: it explicitly tells farmers to talk to their K-State extension agronomist, their NRCS office and their groundwater district before changing a rotation.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

The modelling and backend are written in Python 3.14 with pandas, NumPy, Pydantic and FastAPI, tested with pytest and managed with uv. The frontend is written in TypeScript with React 19, Vite, Leaflet, geotiff.js and proj4. It reads Sentinel-2 Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs from the Microsoft Planetary Computer and computes NDVI directly in the browser. The AI layer uses the Model Context Protocol and Gemini with tool calling. Frontend and API are deployed on Vercel as two services, and the live demo is at https://field-shift-beta.vercel.app.

Our data sources:

- NASA POWER

- Copernicus Sentinel-2

- USDA NASS: Cropland Data Layer, Quick Stats and crop calendars

- USDA NRCS SSURGO and ISRIC SoilGrids

- FAO-56 and FAO Ecocrop

- USGS 3DEP elevation data

- Extension publications from K-State, SARE and NDSU

No special hardware was needed beyond our laptops.

How is your project creative?

Most tools look at one crop in one season. AGRIscora scores whole multi-year rotations, because each crop shapes the next one through soil water, nitrogen credits and disease carry-over. We model cover crops honestly: the triticale takes soil water and changes the next crop's nitrogen need, so the tool shows its real cost next to its erosion benefit. Live Sentinel-2 crop vigour sits beside 35 years of NASA climate history in one view written in plain farmer language. Through MCP, any AI assistant can query, explain and re-rank rotations from the real numbers instead of making them up.

What factors did your team consider?

Scientific accuracy and traceability came first: every parameter comes from a cited source, and every assumption is documented in the code and shown in the UI. We paid attention to agronomic realism:

- realistic planting windows and double-crop timing

- disease rotation limits

- NRCS cover crop termination rules

- cold stress counted only below a crop's absolute minimum temperature, and winter kill counted only for winter wheat during dormancy

We chose to show uncertainty across all weather years rather than a single value. For usability we used US units, plain wording and adjustable priorities, and we made the farmer's own rotation the baseline.

We are open about the current limits:

- every season is assumed to be fully irrigated

- the weather grid is about 50 km wide

- yields are county averages

- triticale is the only cover crop so far

- prices and costs are not part of the comparison yet

- water rights are a topic for future workne
